# poly

**A programming language and runtime for the stateful core of software written by coding agents.**

A poly program is a set of declared state machines. Each machine carries its contract, its invariants, its effects and the obligations that govern it. The compiler checks the program exhaustively over declared finite domains before it may run. The runtime executes the same program durably, gates every effect, and writes a ledger that replays exactly.

poly adds no new checking, simulation or governance engine. It is a compiler, a toolchain and one runtime integration over the Poly stack. Every construct lowers to an artefact an existing engine already reads:

| Stage | Engines |
|---|---|
| Model and check | SAM v2, polygraph, polyrun, polyvers, polynv |
| Govern | Polyaxion, polycheck |
| Workflows | polyflow, polycrew |
| Learn | Polyx, polyness |
| Simulate (v2) | Polytrion |

> Status: specification, draft v0.6 (after five reviews). No code yet.

## Hello, world

A turnstile. Put a coin in, it unlocks; push it, it locks.

```poly
module hello

type Mode = Locked | Unlocked

machine Gate {
  state {
    mode  : Mode = Locked
    coins : 0..3 = 0
  }
  action Coin()
  action Push()

  on Coin {
    require coins < 3 else reject "coin-box-full"
    coins' = coins + 1
    mode' = Unlocked
  }
  on Push {
    require mode is Unlocked else reject "locked"
    mode' = Locked
  }

  invariant locked-when-empty: coins == 0 implies mode is Locked
}
```

```
$ poly check hello.poly
hello.poly:5  PL3201 DEADLOCK  Gate
  no action is accepted in a reachable non-terminal state
  witness (4 steps):
    Coin()   Locked/0   -> Unlocked/1
    Coin()   Unlocked/1 -> Unlocked/2
    Coin()   Unlocked/2 -> Unlocked/3
    Push()   Unlocked/3 -> Locked/3      then Coin: coin-box-full, Push: locked
verdict: FINDINGS (exit 1)  over coins ∈ 0..3; 7 states
```

The invariant holds. What `poly check` finds is that a full coin box locks the turnstile forever. Add an operator action and it is clean:

```poly
  action Empty()
  on Empty {
    require mode is Locked else reject "unlocked"
    coins' = 0
  }
```

Running it from TypeScript takes three lines:

```ts
const rt = await load('./.poly/build')
const gate = await rt.create('hello.Gate')
await rt.dispatch(gate.id, 'Coin', {}, { actionId: 'coin-1' })   // { stepKind: 'accepted', state: { mode: 'Unlocked', coins: 1 } }
```

Handlers are pure functions of the pre-state: a primed field is written, never read. That is why the order of lines inside a handler cannot change what it does. The same machine can also be written as TypeScript with the embedded surface (technical specification, PT2.5).

## A second look: the double charge

```poly
machine Order {
  state {
    status : Status = Draft
    items  : 0..3   = 0
    paid   : bool   = false
  }
  action AddItem()
  action Place()
  action Pay(amount: int check { 10, 20 })

  on Place {
    require status == Draft else reject "not-draft"
    require items > 0      else reject "empty-order"
    status' = Placed
  }
  on Pay(amount) {
    require status == Placed else reject "not-placed"
    emit charge(amount)
  }

  invariant shipped-was-paid: status == Shipped implies paid
  path property charge-at-most-once: count("payment.charge") <= 1

  effect charge(amount: int) {
    kind "payment.charge"
    labels { egress:external }
    class irreversible
    ok -> PaymentOk()
    failed -> PaymentFailed(code: "declined")
  }
}
```

`poly check` finds that two `Pay` calls emit two charges, and says why they can:

```
orders.poly:17  PL4001 PATH_PROPERTY  charge-at-most-once
  witness (4 steps):
    AddItem()      Draft/0  -> Draft/1
    Place()        Draft/1  -> Placed/1
    Pay(10)        Placed/1 -> Placed/1   emits payment.charge
    Pay(10)        Placed/1 -> Placed/1   emits payment.charge   <- count = 2
  test:  poly witness sha256:3be1… --test   (fails on this program)
  fixes: [enter-charging-status]  add status Charging, entered by Pay, left by PaymentOk / PaymentFailed
orders.poly:16  PL4002 EMIT_WITHOUT_STATE_CHANGE  Pay
  Pay emits payment.charge and leaves the state unchanged, so it can repeat its effect without limit
  witness (4 steps):
    AddItem()      Draft/0  -> Draft/1
    Place()        Draft/1  -> Placed/1
    Pay(10)        Placed/1 -> Placed/1   emits payment.charge
    Pay(10)        Placed/1 -> Placed/1   emits payment.charge
  fixes: [enter-charging-status]  record the emission in the state
verdict: FINDINGS (exit 1)  over items ∈ 0..3, amount ∈ {10, 20}
```

Each call is allowed; the sequence is not. The second finding names the cause: a step that emits and changes nothing can always be taken again. That is the bug the Poly stack was built to find, reported before the program can run. The snippet is abridged; the full example is in the technical specification, PT4.5.



## A third look: machines that talk

Machines hold addresses, not each other's state, and talk only by `send`. A **configuration** checks several of them together, with messages arriving in any order. In the checkout example (technical specification, PT7a), an inventory and each order are safe on their own. If the order confirms as soon as it hears "available", two orders can both be confirmed against the last unit:

```
checkout.poly:33  PL5401 CONFIGURATION_INVARIANT  confirmed-within-stock
  witness: Place@order[0], Place@order[1], Query(order[0]) -> inv, Query(order[1]) -> inv,
           Available(1) -> order[0], Available(1) -> order[1]
```

No per-machine check can see this. The defect lives in the arrival order between machines.

## Principles

0. **The semantics is the definition.** 04-semantics says what a program means; every `poly check` validates the lowering against it.
0a. **One program, three interpreters.** The same machine is checked (all inputs), simulated (sampled inputs, v2) and run (real inputs). Only the environment changes.
0b. **Machines talk only by messages.** Addresses are values, `send` is the only way to affect a peer, and interacting machines are checked together as configurations.
1. **The engines check single machines; poly checks how machines relate.** Safety, governance, simulation and mining stay in the engines. poly's own model checker, poly-ref, checks the lowering, deadlock, liveness and configurations.
2. **The checked program is the running program, over its check domains.** A certificate binds the source, the artefacts and the check results by digest. Out-of-domain inputs are rejected (`strict`) or journaled as drift (`disclosed`).

   **Domains refuse by default (S400, PT3.4a).** A check domain on an action's parameter is a constraint: an integer range, an enum, a `bool` or a `check { … }` clause refuses a value outside it at dispatch, with the reason `outside-check-domain`, before the handler runs. Write `disclosed` after a `check` clause (`amount: int check { 1, 2 } disclosed`) to accept values outside the domain and only report them; such a value is then outside what was checked.
3. **One source per machine.** Every engine artefact is derived.
4. **No silent clean.** Every check reports clean, findings, refused, underpowered or inconclusive.
5. **No model call on a check or decision path.**
6. **The journal is the corpus.** Runtime journals feed replay, versioning, mining and simulation unchanged.

## Conclusion

The Poly stack already holds the primitives a coding agent needs to write stateful code that holds. poly makes them one language. The first milestone is a lowering that reproduces the field-study results from poly source. The third is an experiment, run before any runtime is built, that measures escaped defects and cost against the host language alone. The runtime work depends on its result.

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SAM** | State-Action-Model. The pattern every poly machine lowers to, in its v2 strict profile. |
| **Machine** | A sealed state, a set of actions and one handler per action. The unit of checking and of execution. |
| **Handler** | `on Action { … }`. Requires first, then writes. It either accepts or rejects with a named reason. |
| **Check domain** | The finite set of values a field or parameter takes during checking. Narrower than the runtime type when declared so, and strict unless written disclosed (S400). |
| **Invariant** | A predicate on states that holds in every reachable state. |
| **Step property** | A predicate on every accepted step `(pre, action, data, post)`. |
| **Reject property** | A predicate on every step, whatever its verdict. |
| **Path property** | A prefix-closed predicate on the effects emitted along a path, such as `count(k) <= 1`. |
| **Liveness** | A property that something eventually happens, stated with the weak-fairness assumption it needs; its counterexample is a lasso. |
| **Deadlock** | A reachable non-terminal state in which no action is accepted. Checked for every machine. |
| **Checked instance** | The finite set of inputs and states a verdict covers. Every verdict is printed with it. |
| **poly-ref** | poly's model checker: a reference interpreter written from 04-semantics, used for translation validation, deadlock, liveness, configurations and obligation consistency. |
| **Possibility property** | A property that a good path exists (such as a mandate being dischargeable), as opposed to a property of all behaviours. |
| **Trust scope** | The governance scope an instance belongs to. Messages that cross a trust scope pass the gate. |
| **Tagged union** | A type whose values are one of several constructors, each with its own payload. Makes invalid states unrepresentable. |
| **Tri** | The three-valued truth type of policy expressions (true, false, unknown). Machine expressions are `Bool`. |
| **Capability** | An object passed to a handler that grants exactly the authority its effect's labels and targets declare. |
| **Interpretation** | One of three ways to feed the same machine: check (all inputs), simulate (sampled inputs) or run (real inputs). |
| **Embedded surface** | poly written as valid TypeScript with the `poly/embed` combinators; it produces the same AST as the standalone syntax. |
| **Ref** | The address of an instance (`Ref<M>`). It can be stored and passed in messages, but not dereferenced. |
| **Configuration** | A finite set of instances checked together, with messages in transit delivered in any order within a declared bound. |
| **Attached / detached child** | An attached child shares its parent's atomic cascade and kernel shard. A detached child is a separate actor that communicates by messages. |
| **Delivery guarantee** | Every message sent is eventually received: part of the semantics, implemented by the runtime (obligation R1). |
| **Dischargeable** | A mandate is dischargeable when some path reaches its discharge state without a deny under all obligations together. |
| **Kernel assumption** | A property of the runtime (K1 to K8) that a guarantee about running programs depends on. |
| **Witness** | The shortest concrete sequence that violates an invariant or reaches a forbidden region. It can be exported as a trace and as a test. |
| **Effect** | A declared side effect emitted by an accepted step. It carries labels and a class, and passes the gate before it runs. |
| **Label** | A term from a closed vocabulary (for example `egress:external`) that describes what an effect touches. |
| **Obligation** | A rule, machine, invariant or recalled text inside a `policy`, enforced by the Polyaxion gate. |
| **Effect gate** | The Polyaxion guarded merge that decides allow, deny or escalate before an effect or tool call executes. Distinct from the polycheck runtime guard and the polygents gate. |
| **Strict / disclosed** | The two modes of a check domain. `strict` rejects out-of-domain input at dispatch; `disclosed` accepts it and journals it as drift. |
| **Admission** | Passing the check pipeline. Only admitted programs load. |
| **Certificate** | The signed record of what was checked: source digest, artefact digests, check results, domains, stages not run and accepted exceptions. |
| **Ledger** | The signed record of steps, proposals, verdicts, effects, observations and advice, hash-chained per run. |
| **Anchor** | A signed Merkle root over the heads of all runs, published periodically, proving no run was dropped from a period. |
| **Work order** | An effect of a workflow machine, handed to an agent or a person to claim, run and report. |
| **World** | A set of machines, responders and drivers that Polytrion runs against a virtual clock. Deferred to v2. |
| **Lowering** | Compiling a poly construct into the artefact an existing engine reads. |

    mode' = Unlocked

    mode' = Locked
  }

```poly
machine Order {
  state {
    status : Status = Draft
    items  : 0..3   = 0
    paid   : bool   = false
  }
  action AddItem()
  action Place()
  action Pay(amount: int check { 10, 20 })

    require status == Draft else reject "not-draft"
    require items > 0      else reject "empty-order"
    status' = Placed
  }
  on Pay(amount) {
    require status == Placed else reject "not-placed"
    emit charge(amount)
  }

  invariant shipped-was-paid: status == Shipped implies paid
  path property charge-at-most-once: count("payment.charge") <= 1

  effect charge(amount: int) {
    kind "payment.charge"
    labels { egress:external }
    class irreversible
    ok -> PaymentOk()
    failed -> PaymentFailed(code: "declined")
  }

```

Each call is allowed; the sequence is not. The second finding names the cause: a step that emits and changes nothing can always be taken again. ## A third look: machines that talk

Machines hold addresses, not each other's state, and talk only by `send`. A **configuration** checks several of them together, with messages arriving in any order. In the checkout example (technical specification, PT7a), an inventory and each order are safe on their own. ## Principles

0. **The semantics is the definition.** 04-semantics says what a program means; every `poly check` validates the lowering against it.
0a. **One program, three interpreters.** The same machine is checked (all inputs), simulated (sampled inputs, v2) and run (real inputs). Only the environment changes.
0b. **Machines talk only by messages.** Addresses are values, `send` is the only way to affect a peer, and interacting machines are checked together as configurations.
1. **The engines check single machines; poly checks how machines relate.** Safety, governance, simulation and mining stay in the engines. poly's own model checker, poly-ref, checks the lowering, deadlock, liveness and configurations.
2. **The checked program is the running program, over its check domains.** A certificate binds the source, the artefacts and the check results by digest. Out-of-domain inputs are rejected (`strict`) or journaled as drift (`disclosed`).

   **Domains refuse by default (S400, PT3.4a).** A check domain on an action's parameter is a constraint: an integer range, an enum, a `bool` or a `check { … }` clause refuses a value outside it at dispatch, with the reason `outside-check-domain`, before the handler runs. Write `disclosed` after a `check` clause (`amount: int check { 1, 2 } disclosed`) to accept values outside the domain and only report them; such a value is then outside what was checked.
3. **One source per machine.** Every engine artefact is derived.
4. **No silent clean.** Every check reports clean, findings, refused, underpowered or inconclusive.
5. **No model call on a check or decision path.**
6. **The journal is the corpus.** Runtime journals feed replay, versioning, mining and simulation unchanged.

## Conclusion

The Poly stack already holds the primitives a coding agent needs to write stateful code that holds. poly makes them one language. The first milestone is a lowering that reproduces the field-study results from poly source. The third is an experiment, run before any runtime is built, that measures escaped defects and cost against the host language alone. The runtime work depends on its result.

## PS1. Machines and states

- **PS1.1** A machine `M` is a tuple `(F, init, A, H, G, term)`:
  - `F` is a finite, ordered set of fields. Each field `f` has a type `T(f)` and a check domain `D(f) ⊆ T(f)`. The first field is the **control field**.

  - `A` is a finite set of actions. Each action `a` has a parameter record type `T(a)` and a check domain `D(a) ⊆ T(a)`, the product of its parameters' check domains.

  - `G` is the ordered list of guards (`guard all when … reject …`).
  - `term` is the terminal predicate.
- **PS1.2** A **state** is a function `s` from `F` to values with `s(f) ∈ T(f)` for every field. `S` is the set of states. The state contains the declared fields and nothing else: no verdict, no pending effects, no timers.
- **PS1.4** **Types.** The value types are `bool`, integer ranges, `int`, `string`, finite maps with enum keys, and **tagged unions**. A tagged union `U = C1 { p1 } | … | Cn { pn }` has constructors `Ci`, each with a record of named payload fields `pi` (possibly empty). Its values are pairs `(Ci, r)` with `r` a record of the payload types of `Ci`. An enum is a tagged union whose constructors have no payload. A union is finite when every payload field's type or check domain is finite.
- **PS1.5** **The control field may be a union.** `term` then depends only on its constructor. So `terminal intent is Done | Denied | Dead` is a predicate on the tag.
- **PS1.6** **Addresses.** `Ref<M>` is the type of addresses of instances of machine `M`. An address is a value: it can be held in state, carried in a message and compared with `==`. It cannot be dereferenced; nothing can read another instance's state. `none` is the empty address. In a configuration (PS13), the check domain of a `Ref<M>` is the set of addresses of the configuration's `M` instances plus `none`, so it is finite. In a machine checked alone, a `Ref<M>` ranges over `none` and `n` symbolic addresses `M#1 … M#n`, where `n` is the number of `Ref<M>` fields plus the largest number of `Ref<M>` parameters of one action; when `M` is the machine's own type, `self` is one more distinct address (S57), and each key of a detached spawn of `M` adds one more (S78). A detached child's address `<parent>/<k>` is absolute from the commit of the step that creates it (S78). An address is only compared with `==` or passed on, and a state and one step's data hold at most that many addresses of `M`, so every pattern of equalities among them is realised: the check is sound, and it adds no behaviour a real run cannot have.
- **PS1.7** **A machine may be a service.** `service` marks a machine that is never terminal (an inventory, a ledger). It is exempt from the per-instance deadlock check of PS5.6 and is covered by the configuration's quiescence check instead (PS13.6).

## PS2. Handlers denote functions

- **PS2.1** A handler for action `a` denotes a function

  ```
  h_a : S × T(a) → Verdict
  Verdict = accept(w, E) | reject(r)
  ```

  where:
  - `w` is a partial function from fields to values: the writes;
  - `E` is a finite sequence of effect intents (effects, timer sets and cancels, spawns, signals), in statement order;
  - `r` is a reason, a string literal from the handler's text.
- **PS2.2** A handler body is evaluated against the pre-state `s` and the data `d` as follows:
  0. **Names.** A bare name denotes the innermost binding: a local (`let` or a pattern binder), then a parameter of `a` (a component of `d`), then a field (a component of `s`). `pre.f` always denotes `s(f)`, so a field hidden by a parameter of the same name stays readable (S19).
  1. **Guards.** The guards in `G` are evaluated in declaration order, against `s`, `a` and `d`. A guard sees the parameters of `a` only where `action == A` narrows the action; elsewhere a bare name is a field (S19). The first guard whose condition holds yields `reject(r)` with its reason.
  2. **Body.** Statements are evaluated in order:
     - `require c else reject r` yields `reject(r)` if `c` is false and continues otherwise;
     - `reject r` yields `reject(r)`;
     - `let x = e` binds `x`;
     - `if c B1 else B2` evaluates the chosen branch;
     - `f' = e` adds `f ↦ value(e)` to `w`;
     - `f' = f with [k] = v` adds `f ↦ s(f)[k := v]` to `w`. Entry writes to one map on one path combine when their keys are distinct constants after unrolling (literals, constructors, or the index of different copies of a loop): `w(f) = s(f)[k1 := v1][k2 := v2]…` (S55);
     - `match e { C1 {x…} => B1 … _ => Bn }` evaluates `e`, binds the payload of the first arm whose constructor (and literal payload, if written) matches, and evaluates that arm's block. The compiler requires the arms to be exhaustive (`PL1501 NON_EXHAUSTIVE_MATCH`). So `match` never falls through, and handlers stay total;
     - `f' = C { q: e … }` writes a whole union value. A union field is always written as a whole value, never one payload field at a time;

An effect is also a message: `emit k(d)` sends `d` to the host actor that performs kind `k`, whose address is the handler's capability (PS1.6, PT6.5).
  3. **End.** If the body completes without a rejection, the result is `accept(w, E)`.
- **PS2.3** **Expressions read the pre-state only.** A primed field is write-only. Reading `f'` is a compile error (`PL1202 READ_OF_PRIMED_FIELD`). So the order of assignments within a handler does not change the result.
- **PS2.4** A field written twice on one control path is `PL2102 DOUBLE_WRITE`. A map is written twice when it is assigned twice, assigned and also written by entry, written twice at one constant key, or written at a key that is a field or a parameter on a path that writes another of its entries (S55). Therefore `w` is well defined.
- **PS2.5** All expressions are total (PT2.2): integer division truncates toward zero, `%` takes the sign of the dividend, and a divisor that may be 0 is rejected at compile time (`PL1204`). So `h_a` is a total function. **A machine is deterministic in its inputs**: for each state and each input there is exactly one verdict.

## PS3. Steps and the transition relation

- **PS3.1** A **label** is a triple `(a, d, v)` of an action, its data and a verdict kind:
  - `v = accepted(E)`;
  - `v = rejected(r)`;
  - `v = unhandled`.
- **PS3.2** The transition relation `R_M ⊆ S × Label × S` contains exactly these triples `(s, (a, d, v), s')`, for every `s ∈ S`, `a ∈ A` and `d ∈ T(a)`:

  | Condition | Verdict `v` | Next state `s'` |
  |---|---|---|
  | `term(s)` | `rejected("terminal")` | `s` |
  | `d` violates a `strict` check domain of `a` (PT3.4) | `rejected("outside-check-domain")` | `s` |
  | `a ∉ dom(H)` | `unhandled` | `s` |
  | `h_a(s, d) = reject(r)` | `rejected(r)` | `s` |
  | `h_a(s, d) = accept(w, E)` | `accepted(E)` | `s ⊕ w` |

  `(s ⊕ w)(f) = w(f)` if `f ∈ dom(w)`, and `s(f)` otherwise. This is the **frame**: every field not written is unchanged.
- **PS3.3** **Rejected and unhandled steps are steps.** They are transitions whose next state equals their current state, and they carry their verdict in the label, not in the state. They are journaled, they appear in traces, and properties over labels see them (PS5). Properties over states cannot distinguish them from not taking a step at all. This is the answer to the question "is a rejected step a step?": it is a labelled stuttering step.
- **PS3.4** An accepted step may leave the state unchanged (for example `Pay` in PT4.5, which only emits). It is still accepted, and its label carries its effects.

- **PS4.1** The **environment** chooses each action and its data. A **path** is a finite sequence `s0 l0 s1 l1 … sn` with `s0 = init` and `(si, li, si+1) ∈ R_M` for every `i`. A **behaviour** is an infinite such sequence.

For fields in `strict` mode, **run** cannot offer an input outside `D(a)`, because the runtime rejects it before the handler (PS3.2), so the condition holds by construction. For fields in `disclosed` mode, the theorem covers exactly the paths whose inputs stayed in the domain, and the others are journaled as drift. ∎ So every safety property that is `CLEAN` on **check** holds on every such **run** path.
- **PS4.1c** A Polytrion world (v2) is a definition of **simulate** for a set of machines. The machines are unchanged. This is the formal content of the Polytrion principle "responders draw, machines decide, the kernel schedules".
- **PS4.1d** In **check**, the environment is unconstrained: every action, with every data value in its domain, may be offered in every state.
- **PS4.1e** **The bounded fragment.** Checks cover finite instances: finite domains, a finite number of instances, and a declared bound on messages in transit (PS13). The actor guarantee that a message is delivered after an unbounded but finite delay cannot be expressed in a finite instance. Liveness checks approximate it with fairness (PS6, PS14). The runtime implements the unbounded guarantee (R1, PS10).
- **PS4.2** The **checked instance** `I` restricts inputs to their check domains (every `d ∈ D(a)`) and states to theirs: a state is **in the instance** when every field `f` has `s(f) ∈ D(f)`. `Reach(I)` is the set of in-instance states on paths of `I` that stay in the instance. It is finite, because every field type in a checked machine is finite or restricted to a finite check domain (PT3.2).
- **PS4.2a** **Leaving the instance.** A transition from a state in `Reach(I)` can produce a post-state outside the instance in two ways, and they mean different things:
  - **Outside a declared type.** The post-state writes a value outside a field's declared type, such as `items: 0..3` becoming 4. The post-state is not in `S` at all. This is a program error: `PL3102 DOMAIN_ESCAPE`, a finding, with the path to the transition (PT3.5).
  - **Outside a check domain only.** The post-state stays inside the declared type (`int` or `string`) but leaves the field's check domain, such as a `term: int check 0..3` becoming 4. The post-state is a legal state that the instance does not cover. This is a **bound hit**: `PL3901 BOUND_HIT`, naming the field, with the shortest path to the boundary. The post-state is not explored, and the verdict is at best `INCONCLUSIVE`.

  Properties are still checked on every explored state, so a violation found inside the bound is still reported, and the fold of PT12.3 makes that verdict `FINDINGS`. A counter that grows without limit in the real system (a raft term, a coin count) is therefore checked up to its declared bound, and the verdict says so; it is never `CLEAN`.
- **PS4.3** **Every verdict is about `I`.** A `CLEAN` result states that a property holds on `Reach(I)` and on all paths of `I`. The instance is printed with the verdict (PT12.3a).
- **PS4.4** **Completion actions are ordinary actions.** In `I`, a completion such as `PaymentOk` can be offered in any state, whether or not a charge was emitted. So `I` over-approximates the real system: every real behaviour is a behaviour of `I`, but not every behaviour of `I` is real. For safety properties this is sound: a clean result holds for the real system. A witness may be infeasible if it uses a completion with no matching intent. Such a witness is marked `environment: unconstrained`, and the matching path property check (PS5.4) is the place to rule it out. A `send` is an intent in `E` like any other: a machine checked alone has no receivers, so the replies its receivers would send are ordinary actions the environment may offer in any state. This over-approximates too, and the configuration check (PS13) is where the receivers' actual behaviour is used (S30).

## PS5. Properties

There are five kinds of property. Each has its own keyword (PT5), and none is called an invariant unless it is one.

- **PS5.1** An **invariant** is a predicate `P` on states. `M ⊨ invariant P` iff `P(s)` holds for every `s ∈ Reach(I)`. The automatic `domain:<field>` properties (PT3.5) are invariants.
- **PS5.2** A **step property** is a predicate `Q(s, a, d, s')`. It holds iff `Q` holds for every **accepted** transition from a state in `Reach(I)`. `Q` reads `d` only where `action == A` narrows the action, with the names of PS2.2 (S19).
- **PS5.3** A **reject property** is a predicate `J(s, a, d, v)`. It holds iff `J` holds for **every** transition from a state in `Reach(I)`, whatever its verdict. `rejected(r)` in `J` is true iff `v = rejected(r)`. `J` reads `d` only where `action == A` narrows the action; elsewhere a bare name is a field of `s` (PS2.2, S19).
- **PS5.4** A **path property** is a predicate `Φ(π)` on finite paths. It is evaluated through `emitted(π)`, the concatenation of the intent sequences of the accepted labels of `π`, and `actions(π)`, the sequence of actions. It holds iff `Φ(π)` holds for every path `π` of `I`. Path properties must be **prefix-closed**: if `Φ` holds of a path, it holds of every prefix. The compiler accepts only forms that are prefix-closed by construction: `count(k) <= n`, `count(k) < n` (read as `count(k) <= n - 1`), `before(k1, k2)`, and their conjunctions. `count(k)` is the number of intents of kind `k` in `emitted(π)`, and `before(k1, k2)` holds iff every intent of kind `k2` in `emitted(π)` is preceded by an intent of kind `k1` (S37). Any other form is `PL1701 NOT_PREFIX_CLOSED`. So a path property is a safety property and has a finite witness.
- **PS5.5** A **liveness property** has one of two forms:
  - `eventually P`: every fair behaviour of `I` reaches a state satisfying `P`;
  - `P leads to Q`: in every fair behaviour, every state satisfying `P` is followed by a state satisfying `Q`.

  Fairness is defined in PS6. A liveness property is not a safety property and has no finite witness. Its counterexample is a **lasso**: a path to a cycle that can repeat forever.
- **PS5.6** **Deadlock.** A state `s ∈ Reach(I)` is a **deadlock** iff `¬term(s)` and no action accepts in `s`: for every `a` and every `d ∈ D(a)`, the verdict is not `accepted`. Deadlock freedom is checked for every machine, whether or not it declares a liveness property (`PL3201 DEADLOCK`, with the path to the state).

## PS6. Fairness

- **PS6.1** An action group `g` is a set of actions (written `A | B`). `g` is **enabled** in `s` iff some `a ∈ g` and some `d ∈ D(a)` give an accepted transition from `s`. `A(*)` in a fairness list stands for one group per data value: `{A(d)}` for each `d ∈ D(A)`. So `Send(*)` is fair to each message separately, and a sender that keeps sending one value cannot starve another.
- **PS6.2** A behaviour is **weakly fair for `g`**, written `WF(g)`, iff `g` is not enabled continuously from some point on without an accepted step of `g` being taken infinitely often. In words: an action group that stays enabled is eventually taken.
- **PS6.3** A liveness property is always stated with its fairness assumption: `liveness n: eventually P under fair { g1, g2, … }`. It is checked only over behaviours that are weakly fair for every listed group. Actions not listed carry no assumption: the environment may never offer them. A person's approval, for example, is not listed.
- **PS6.3a** Liveness under fairness is a game. The environment is an adversary that chooses inputs, constrained only by the stated fairness. A liveness property holds when the adversary has no strategy that avoids `P` forever. The lasso of PS6.4 is the adversary's winning strategy.
- **PS6.4** **Check.** Over the finite graph of `Reach(I)`, `eventually P` fails iff there is a strongly connected component `C`, of the states reachable from the initial state through states where `P` does not hold, with all of the following properties (S82):
  1. `C` contains no `P`-state.
  2. `C` contains at least one edge, where rejected and unhandled steps count as edges.
  3. For every listed group `g`, either some edge of `C` is an accepted step of `g`, or `g` is disabled in some state of `C`.

  This is the standard component test for weak fairness on a finite graph. `P leads to Q` is checked by the same test on the graph restricted to the part after a `P`-state, until `Q`. The counterexample is the path to `C` followed by a cycle through `C` that visits every edge the third condition names.

## PS7. Composition

Children come in two kinds. The author chooses, and the verdict says which semantics was checked.

- **PS7.1** **Attached children** (the default) form a **joint machine** with their parent. Its state is `(s_P, {k ↦ s_k})`, over the children spawned so far, and with each instance's status (active or terminal) and each child's wiring (its completion and cancel actions). The joint label is the **stimulus** `(target, a, d)`, where the target is the parent or a child key. The stimuli are offered as the kernel delivers them (S45): a terminal instance is offered nothing, and an action wired as the completion of a child is offered to the parent only once that child is terminal, because until then only the kernel delivers it, in the cascade. Inside a cascade, a delivery to a terminal instance is rejected and changes nothing. This rests on kernel assumption K9.
- **PS7.2** A joint step of attached children is the **cascade** of a stimulus: the stimulus's own transition, followed by every transition it causes, applied in order. These are completions to the parent, parent-terminal actions to children and signals, up to depth 8. The joint step is accepted iff the stimulus transition is accepted. A cascade that exceeds depth 8 is `PL5201 CASCADE_DEPTH`.
- **PS7.3** A **compose invariant** is an invariant (PS5.1) of the joint machine.
- **PS7.4** **Attached means co-located.** The cascade semantics is a model of the runtime only under K1 to K3, and K3 (one transaction per cascade) holds only if the parent and all its attached descendants are served by one kernel shard. The runtime shards by the root of each attached tree and refuses to place an attached child elsewhere (`PL5202 ATTACHED_ACROSS_SHARDS`). Every composition guarantee cites K1 to K3 and this rule.
- **PS7.5** **Detached children** (`spawn detached …`) are separate actors. `spawn` creates the instance and returns its address to the parent. From then on, parent and child communicate only by messages (`send`), which may arrive in any order. Their composition is checked as a configuration (PS13), not as a cascade.

## PS8. Policies

- **PS8.0** **Two truth types.** `Bool = {T, F}`. `Tri = {T, F, U}`, which is `Bool` lifted into an option type, with Kleene's rules for the missing case. The inputs a policy reads (the proposal, the action's labels, `machine(…)` fields, history) have **optional types**: any of them may be missing. A comparison or boolean operator applied to an optional operand has type `Tri`. Machine fields are never optional, so every machine expression has type `Bool`. `unknown(x)` has type `Bool`. A machine `require` demands `Bool`. A policy `when` or `require` accepts `Tri` and is evaluated by PS8.2. A `Tri` where a `Bool` is expected is a type error (`PL1203 TRI_WHERE_BOOL_EXPECTED`). The two logics are separated by type. One set of operators (`==`, `!=`, `&&`, `||`, `!`) serves both, and its meaning follows the operand types.
- **PS8.1** Policy expressions take values in `{T, F, U}`, where `U` is unknown.
  - `not`, `and` and `or` follow Kleene's strong three-valued logic: `not U = U`; `F and U = F`; `T and U = U`; `T or U = T`; `F or U = U`.
  - A comparison with an unknown operand is `U`.
  - `unknown(x)` is `T` or `F`, never `U`.
- **PS8.2** A `rule` obligation `when W require Q else s on unknown u` is evaluated for a proposal as follows. The severity `s` is `deny`, `warn` or `escalate`. The unknown handling `u` is `escalate`, `deny` or `skip`.

  | `W` | `Q` | Outcome |
  |---|---|---|
  | `F` | any | not applicable |
  | `T` | `T` | satisfied |
  | `T` | `F` or `U` | `s` (an unknown value never satisfies a requirement) |
  | `U` | any | `u` |

  **The default for `u`:**
  - For `s = deny`, the default is `escalate`. A deny rule whose condition cannot be evaluated never passes silently.
  - For `s = warn`, the default is `warn`.
  - `skip` must be written explicitly. It is listed in the certificate under `skippedOnUnknown`.
- **PS8.3** **Combination.** The gate's decision for a proposal is:
  - `deny` if any obligation's outcome is `deny`;
  - otherwise `escalate` if any outcome is `escalate`;
  - otherwise `allow`.

  Warnings are recorded with an `allow`.
- **PS8.4** **Labels.** In a scope where any obligation mentions `effects`, `labels` or `class`, an effect or tool with no labels is **refused at admission** (`PL6302 UNLABELLED_IN_LABELLED_SCOPE`, verdict `REFUSED`). An unlabelled effect cannot make a label-based rule's `when` unknown at runtime.
- **PS8.5** `machine("<module>.<Machine>").f` is the value of `f` in the post-state of the step that emitted the effect under decision (PT9.3). It is `U` for a proposal that is not an effect of that machine.
- **PS8.6** **Consistency of obligations.** Obligations in one scope come from several sources: declared policies, promoted Polyx rules, recalled text and native kernels. Each decision is resolved by PS8.3, but the obligations may still contradict each other as a whole. A mandate `m` is **dischargeable** under a set of obligations `O` iff some path over the scope's **tool alphabet** reaches a discharge state of `m` with no `deny` outcome on the way. The tool alphabet is the set of actions the scope's tools can perform, with their labels. The declared action alphabet is used only when the scope has no tool catalogue, and the certificate records which alphabet was used. This is Polyaxion's admission condition m2, "lawfully dischargeable".
  - **A possibility property.** Dischargeability says that a good path *exists*. Every other property in this document constrains *all* behaviours. It is not a property of behaviours: a system whose behaviours all satisfy every PS5 property may fail it, and the converse. It is checked as reachability on the explored graph of the scope's policy machines, not with the machinery of PS5 and PS6, and diagnostics name it as a possibility property.
  - If `m` is not dischargeable, the finding (`PL6501 UNDISCHARGEABLE_MANDATE`) names **a minimal conflicting subset** `O' ⊆ O`: `m` is not dischargeable under `O'`, and it is dischargeable under `O' \ {o}` for every `o ∈ O'`. It is minimal, not necessarily smallest. Different deletion orders can find different minimal subsets, so the order is fixed for reproducibility: obligations are tried for removal in declaration order, then promoted rules in promotion order.
  - The check runs at admission and again on **every promotion** of a mined rule, because promotion is when rules written from different evidence first meet.

- **PS8.7** **Which messages cross the gate.** Every instance has a **trust scope**: the scope of its module's policy, or the scope its configuration assigns to it.
  - A `send` whose sender and receiver are in **different** trust scopes is proposed to the gate, exactly like an effect. A send within one scope is not.
  - Effects to capability addresses are always proposed, as before (PT9).
  - **A denied send** is not delivered. Instead, the message `SendDenied(to, action, reason)` is delivered to the sender itself, as an ordinary message. The sender may handle it; if it has no handler, it is an unhandled step, journaled like any other. A denied send is therefore visible in the sender's behaviour and in the checked configuration, where the gate's decision is an environment choice among allow, deny and escalate (PS4.4).
  - Governance thus sees every message that leaves a trust scope. "One mechanism" holds for control as well as for execution.

## PS9. Lowering correctness

- **PS9.1** Let `L(M)` be the lowered module. Let `R_L` be its transition relation under the SAM v2 strict profile. For each `(s, a, d)`:
  - an acceptor rejecting with `r` gives `rejected(r)`;
  - writes to `next`, with the declared `unchanged`, give the next state;
  - the effects mapper applied to the step gives `E`.
- **PS9.1a** The first two rows of the table in PS3.2 (terminal states and strict check domains) are applied by the runtime before it calls the module. `R_L` is therefore the module's relation with those two rules applied first, exactly as the runtime applies them. An action with no handler is not in the module's action surface (S35), so the runtime answers it without calling the module: row 1, `rejected("terminal")`, in a terminal state, and row 3, `unhandled`, elsewhere (row 2 never applies: a parameter is `strict` by default only when a handler lets it flow into an effect, and an explicit `strict` on a parameter of an action with no handler is `PL1302 STRICT_ON_UNHANDLED_ACTION`, S53). Those steps are part of `R_L` and are compared like any other.
- **PS9.1b** **Flattening unions.** A union field `f` lowers to a tag field `f` plus one nullable field `f_<payload>` per payload name of any constructor, because the SAM sealed shape is flat. Below the top of a field, where no flat key exists (a map's value, a payload, a parameter), a union with payloads lowers to one object `{ "$": "C", p: v, … }` with exactly its constructor's payloads, recursively, and `α` reads it back; a union with no payload is its constructor's name (S65). Constructors that share a payload name share its field, which requires the same type (`PL1601 PAYLOAD_TYPE_CONFLICT` otherwise). The abstraction function `α` maps a flat state back to a structured one. The lowering adds one automatic invariant per union field (`shape:f`): the payload fields of the current constructor are present, and all others are null. PS9.2 compares `R_M` with `R_L` through `α`.
- **PS9.2** **The lowering is correct for `M` on `I`** iff `R_L` and `R_M` agree on every `(s, a, d)` with `s ∈ Reach(I)` and `d ∈ D(a)`. They must give the same verdict kind, the same reason, the same next state and the same intent sequence. The lowered property modules must also agree with PS5 on every reachable state and transition.
- **PS9.3** **Translation validation on every check.** `poly check` runs `poly-ref`, poly's own model checker and reference interpreter, written directly from this document and sharing no code with the compiler. It explores `I` and compares every transition with the lowered module's. A difference is `PL2501 LOWERING_MISMATCH`. The verdict is `REFUSED`, and the diagnostic is addressed to the toolchain, not to the author. This makes the lowering's correctness a checked fact for each program, not a claim about the compiler.

## PS10. Kernel assumptions

The guarantees about running programs hold under these assumptions about the runtime. Each guarantee in PT and 02 cites the assumptions it uses. Each assumption names its evidence.

| Id | Assumption | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| K1 | **Atomic step.** Snapshot, journal entry, outbox, timers and dedupe key commit in one transaction. | polyrun specification FR on dispatch; polyrun store tests |
| K2 | **Single writer.** At most one step per instance is in flight. | polyrun specification; composition semantics document |
| K3 | **Atomic cascade**, depth at most 8. | polyrun composition semantics |
| K4 | **Idempotent dispatch, for the life of the instance.** A repeated `actionId` returns the recorded result and takes no step, for as long as the instance exists. Archiving keeps the dedupe record: archived instances keep their `(instance, actionId)` keys in a compact tombstone table. A redelivery to an archived instance returns the recorded result, or `archived` for a key it never saw, and never takes a step. | polyrun dedupe table (`UNIQUE(instance_id, action_id)`) |

108	
109	There are five kinds of property. Each has its own keyword (PT5), and none is called an invariant unless it is one.
110	
111	- **PS5.1** An **invariant** is a predicate `P` on states. `M ⊨ invariant P` iff `P(s)` holds for every `s ∈ Reach(I)`. The automatic `domain:<field>` properties (PT3.5) are invariants.
112	- **PS5.2** A **step property** is a predicate `Q(s, a, d, s')`. It holds iff `Q` holds for every **accepted** transition from a state in `Reach(I)`. `Q` reads `d` only where `action == A` narrows the action, with the names of PS2.2 (S19).
113	- **PS5.3** A **reject property** is a predicate `J(s, a, d, v)`. It holds iff `J` holds for **every** transition from a state in `Reach(I)`, whatever its verdict. `rejected(r)` in `J` is true iff `v = rejected(r)`. `J` reads `d` only where `action == A` narrows the action; elsewhere a bare name is a field of `s` (PS2.2, S19).
114	- **PS5.4** A **path property** is a predicate `Φ(π)` on finite paths. It is evaluated through `emitted(π)`, the concatenation of the intent sequences of the accepted labels of `π`, and `actions(π)`, the sequence of actions. It holds iff `Φ(π)` holds for every path `π` of `I`. Path properties must be **prefix-closed**: if `Φ` holds of a path, it holds of every prefix. The compiler accepts only forms that are prefix-closed by construction: `count(k) <= n`, `count(k) < n` (read as `count(k) <= n - 1`), `before(k1, k2)`, and their conjunctions. `count(k)` is the number of intents of kind `k` in `emitted(π)`, and `before(k1, k2)` holds iff every intent of kind `k2` in `emitted(π)` is preceded by an intent of kind `k1` (S37). Any other form is `PL1701 NOT_PREFIX_CLOSED`. So a path property is a safety property and has a finite witness.
115	- **PS5.5** A **liveness property** has one of two forms:
116	  - `eventually P`: every fair behaviour of `I` reaches a state satisfying `P`;
117	  - `P leads to Q`: in every fair behaviour, every state satisfying `P` is followed by a state satisfying `Q`.
118	
119	  Fairness is defined in PS6. A liveness property is not a safety property and has no finite witness. Its counterexample is a **lasso**: a path to a cycle that can repeat forever.
120	- **PS5.6** **Deadlock.** A state `s ∈ Reach(I)` is a **deadlock** iff `¬term(s)` and no action accepts in `s`: for every `a` and every `d ∈ D(a)`, the verdict is not `accepted`. 122	## PS6. Fairness
123	
124	- **PS6.1** An action group `g` is a set of actions (written `A | B`). `g` is **enabled** in `s` iff some `a ∈ g` and some `d ∈ D(a)` give an accepted transition from `s`. `A(*)` in a fairness list stands for one group per data value: `{A(d)}` for each `d ∈ D(A)`. So `Send(*)` is fair to each message separately, and a sender that keeps sending one value cannot starve another.
125	- **PS6.2** A behaviour is **weakly fair for `g`**, written `WF(g)`, iff `g` is not enabled continuously from some point on without an accepted step of `g` being taken infinitely often. In words: an action group that stays enabled is eventually taken.
126	- **PS6.3** A liveness property is always stated with its fairness assumption: `liveness n: eventually P under fair { g1, g2, … }`. It is checked only over behaviours that are weakly fair for every listed group. Actions not listed carry no assumption: the environment may never offer them. A person's approval, for example, is not listed.
127	- **PS6.3a** Liveness under fairness is a game. The environment is an adversary that chooses inputs, constrained only by the stated fairness. A liveness property holds when the adversary has no strategy that avoids `P` forever. The lasso of PS6.4 is the adversary's winning strategy.
128	- **PS6.4** **Check.** Over the finite graph of `Reach(I)`, `eventually P` fails iff there is a strongly connected component `C`, of the states reachable from the initial state through states where `P` does not hold, with all of the following properties (S82):
129	  1. `C` contains no `P`-state.
130	  2. `C` contains at least one edge, where rejected and unhandled steps count as edges.
131	  3. For every listed group `g`, either some edge of `C` is an accepted step of `g`, or `g` is disabled in some state of `C`.
132	
133	  This is the standard component test for weak fairness on a finite graph. `P leads to Q` is checked by the same test on the graph restricted to the part after a `P`-state, until `Q`. The counterexample is the path to `C` followed by a cycle through `C` that visits every edge the third condition names.

135	## PS7. Composition
136	
137	Children come in two kinds. The author chooses, and the verdict says which semantics was checked.
138	
139	- **PS7.1** **Attached children** (the default) form a **joint machine** with their parent. Its state is `(s_P, {k ↦ s_k})`, over the children spawned so far, and with each instance's status (active or terminal) and each child's wiring (its completion and cancel actions). The joint label is the **stimulus** `(target, a, d)`, where the target is the parent or a child key. The stimuli are offered as the kernel delivers them (S45): a terminal instance is offered nothing, and an action wired as the completion of a child is offered to the parent only once that child is terminal, because until then only the kernel delivers it, in the cascade. Inside a cascade, a delivery to a terminal instance is rejected and changes nothing. This rests on kernel assumption K9.
140	- **PS7.2** A joint step of attached children is the **cascade** of a stimulus: the stimulus's own transition, followed by every transition it causes, applied in order. These are completions to the parent, parent-terminal actions to children and signals, up to depth 8. The joint step is accepted iff the stimulus transition is accepted. A cascade that exceeds depth 8 is `PL5201 CASCADE_DEPTH`.
141	- **PS7.3** A **compose invariant** is an invariant (PS5.1) of the joint machine.
142	- **PS7.4** **Attached means co-located.** The cascade semantics is a model of the runtime only under K1 to K3, and K3 (one transaction per cascade) holds only if the parent and all its attached descendants are served by one kernel shard. The runtime shards by the root of each attached tree and refuses to place an attached child elsewhere (`PL5202 ATTACHED_ACROSS_SHARDS`). Every composition guarantee cites K1 to K3 and this rule.
143	- **PS7.5** **Detached children** (`spawn detached …`) are separate actors. `spawn` creates the instance and returns its address to the parent. From then on, parent and child communicate only by messages (`send`), which may arrive in any order. Their composition is checked as a configuration (PS13), not as a cascade.

146	
147	- **PS8.0** **Two truth types.** `Bool = {T, F}`. `Tri = {T, F, U}`, which is `Bool` lifted into an option type, with Kleene's rules for the missing case. The inputs a policy reads (the proposal, the action's labels, `machine(…)` fields, history) have **optional types**: any of them may be missing. A comparison or boolean operator applied to an optional operand has type `Tri`. Machine fields are never optional, so every machine expression has type `Bool`. `unknown(x)` has type `Bool`. A machine `require` demands `Bool`. A policy `when` or `require` accepts `Tri` and is evaluated by PS8.2. A `Tri` where a `Bool` is expected is a type error (`PL1203 TRI_WHERE_BOOL_EXPECTED`). The two logics are separated by type. One set of operators (`==`, `!=`, `&&`, `||`, `!`) serves both, and its meaning follows the operand types.
148	- **PS8.1** Policy expressions take values in `{T, F, U}`, where `U` is unknown.
149	  - `not`, `and` and `or` follow Kleene's strong three-valued logic: `not U = U`; `F and U = F`; `T and U = U`; `T or U = T`; `F or U = U`.
150	  - A comparison with an unknown operand is `U`.
151	  - `unknown(x)` is `T` or `F`, never `U`.
152	- **PS8.2** A `rule` obligation `when W require Q else s on unknown u` is evaluated for a proposal as follows. The severity `s` is `deny`, `warn` or `escalate`. The unknown handling `u` is `escalate`, `deny` or `skip`.
153	
154	  | `W` | `Q` | Outcome |
155	  |---|---|---|
156	  | `F` | any | not applicable |
157	  | `T` | `T` | satisfied |
158	  | `T` | `F` or `U` | `s` (an unknown value never satisfies a requirement) |
159	  | `U` | any | `u` |
160	
161	  **The default for `u`:**
162	  - For `s = deny`, the default is `escalate`. A deny rule whose condition cannot be evaluated never passes silently.
163	  - For `s = warn`, the default is `warn`.
164	  - `skip` must be written explicitly. It is listed in the certificate under `skippedOnUnknown`.
165	- **PS8.3** **Combination.** The gate's decision for a proposal is:
166	  - `deny` if any obligation's outcome is `deny`;
167	  - otherwise `escalate` if any outcome is `escalate`;
168	  - otherwise `allow`.

170	  Warnings are recorded with an `allow`.
171	- **PS8.4** **Labels.** In a scope where any obligation mentions `effects`, `labels` or `class`, an effect or tool with no labels is **refused at admission** (`PL6302 UNLABELLED_IN_LABELLED_SCOPE`, verdict `REFUSED`). 172	- **PS8.5** `machine("<module>.<Machine>").f` is the value of `f` in the post-state of the step that emitted the effect under decision (PT9.3). It is `U` for a proposal that is not an effect of that machine.

A mandate `m` is **dischargeable** under a set of obligations `O` iff some path over the scope's **tool alphabet** reaches a discharge state of `m` with no `deny` outcome on the way. The tool alphabet is the set of actions the scope's tools can perform, with their labels. The declared action alphabet is used only when the scope has no tool catalogue, and the certificate records which alphabet was used. This is Polyaxion's admission condition m2, "lawfully dischargeable".

184	## PS9. Lowering correctness
185	
186	- **PS9.1** Let `L(M)` be the lowered module. Let `R_L` be its transition relation under the SAM v2 strict profile. For each `(s, a, d)`:
187	  - an acceptor rejecting with `r` gives `rejected(r)`;
188	  - writes to `next`, with the declared `unchanged`, give the next state;
189	  - the effects mapper applied to the step gives `E`.
190	- **PS9.1a** The first two rows of the table in PS3.2 (terminal states and strict check domains) are applied by the runtime before it calls the module. `R_L` is therefore the module's relation with those two rules applied first, exactly as the runtime applies them. An action with no handler is not in the module's action surface (S35), so the runtime answers it without calling the module: row 1, `rejected("terminal")`, in a terminal state, and row 3, `unhandled`, elsewhere (row 2 never applies: a parameter is `strict` by default only when a handler lets it flow into an effect, and an explicit `strict` on a parameter of an action with no handler is `PL1302 STRICT_ON_UNHANDLED_ACTION`, S53). 191	- **PS9.1b** **Flattening unions.** A union field `f` lowers to a tag field `f` plus one nullable field `f_<payload>` per payload name of any constructor, because the SAM sealed shape is flat. Below the top of a field, where no flat key exists (a map's value, a payload, a parameter), a union with payloads lowers to one object `{ "$": "C", p: v, … }` with exactly its constructor's payloads, recursively, and `α` reads it back; a union with no payload is its constructor's name (S65). Constructors that share a payload name share its field, which requires the same type (`PL1601 PAYLOAD_TYPE_CONFLICT` otherwise). The abstraction function `α` maps a flat state back to a structured one. The lowering adds one automatic invariant per union field (`shape:f`): the payload fields of the current constructor are present, and all others are null. PS9.2 compares `R_M` with `R_L` through `α`.

219	## PS11. The gate and replay
220	
221	- **PS11.0** **The gate is an actor.** It has its own state (Σ per session), it processes one proposal or settle at a time per session, and its only inputs are messages. The order that determines its decisions is its own **arrival order**, recorded as `sseq`. No global order exists, and none is needed. It follows that:
222	  - a session is a serialisation point: all proposals of a session queue at one actor, and throughput is measured per session (PT9.6);
223	  - the gate can be sharded along sessions, and only along sessions;
224	  - a policy that needs state across sessions needs another actor, reached by messages. It cannot share a variable.
225	
226	- **PS11.1** Each gate session has a **session sequence** `sseq`. The gate assigns it on receipt of every proposal and every settle. Each ledger event carries its `sseq` and the digest of Σ before the event.
227	- **PS11.2** **Replay of a session** re-applies its events in `sseq` order. It must reproduce every decision and every Σ digest. By K6, this reproduces the gate's behaviour exactly.
228	- **PS11.3** **Replay of a run** reproduces every post-state from the run's own chain (K1, PS2.5). It reproduces gate decisions when the sessions the run touched are replayed with it.
229	- **PS11.4** **Replay is a fold.** A run's state after `n` steps is `foldl δ init [l0 … ln-1]`, where `δ(s, (a, d, _))` is the next state given by `R_M`. The replay theorem is then one line: `δ` is a function (PS2.5), so the same journal gives the same fold. The runtime stores the journal, and the state is the fold's cache (the snapshot). A snapshot that disagrees with the fold is a kernel fault, not a program fault.

254	- **PS13.2** A **global state** is a pair `(σ, μ)`:
255	  - `σ` maps each instance to its state;
256	  - `μ` is the **set of identified messages** in transit. Each message is `(id, target, action, data)`. Its identity is `id = (sender, sender's step number, position among that step's intents)`, the model's image of the runtime's idempotency key.
257	- **PS13.2a** **Copies are indistinguishable to the receiver.** Two messages with the same `(target, action, data)` produce the same step at the receiver, whatever their identities. The explorer therefore keeps `μ` as a multiset of values, and a delivery of a value consumes its **oldest** copy. This quotient loses no behaviour: every delivery sequence of identified messages maps to one with the same states and labels. So it is exact for safety.
258	- **PS13.2b** **Fairness per identified message.** In the quotient, weak fairness of each value's delivery, together with oldest-copy delivery, implies that every identified message is eventually delivered. Proof: while a value `v` is in transit, its deliveries are enabled. Weak fairness makes them happen repeatedly. Each delivery removes the oldest copy. A given copy has at most `B - 1` copies ahead of it (PS13.5), so it is delivered after at most `B` deliveries of `v`. ∎ Liveness checks use this fairness (PS14.2).
259	- **PS13.3** A **global step** is one of:
260	  - **input**: the environment injects a declared input `(i, a, d)`;
261	  - **delivery**: any one message in `μ` is removed and delivered to its target.
262	
263	  In either case the target takes its step by `R_M` (PS3.2). The intents of an accepted step are handled as follows:
264	  - its `send` messages are added to `μ`; a send to `none` adds nothing and is a finding (`PL5404 SEND_TO_NONE`, S29);
265	  - its detached `spawn` intents create new instances, each at the address `<parent address>/<k>`, in its machine's initial state, with its creation action as its first message; instances spawned from `M` join the group `M`, and `N` counts every instance (S60). A spawn of a key whose instance already exists creates nothing and is `PL5101 CHILDKEY_COLLISION`, checked before the instance bound (S83);
266	  - its other effects and its timers are completed by the environment only through the configuration's declared inputs: a completion action not listed there is never offered (S61).
267	
268	  A delivery to an instance that rejects the message is a rejected step: the message is consumed and the state is unchanged.
269	- **PS13.4** **Arrival order is nondeterministic.** Any message in transit may be delivered next, whatever order the messages were sent in. This is the only order a configuration assumes. Two messages from one sender to one receiver are not assumed to arrive in order unless the configuration declares `fifo` for that pair.
270	- **PS13.5** **Bounds are reported, never silently applied.** A step that would exceed `B` messages in transit or `N` instances is not explored. The verdict is then at best `INCONCLUSIVE`, with `PL5301 TRANSIT_BOUND_HIT` or `PL5302 INSTANCE_BOUND_HIT` and the bound. It is never `CLEAN`.
271	- **PS13.6** **Properties of a configuration.**
272	  - A **configuration invariant** is a predicate on `σ`.
273	  - **Instance groups and quantifiers.** `g[*]` may appear only as the argument of an aggregate: `count`, `sum`, `all` or `any`. Everywhere else a group must be quantified explicitly: `forall i in g: P(g[i])` or `exists i in g: P(g[i])`. An unquantified `g[*]` outside an aggregate is `PL5403 UNQUANTIFIED_GROUP`. In a liveness property, the quantifier scopes over the whole `leads to`: `forall i in order: order[i] is Asked leads to order[i] is Done | Refused` means that each asked order is eventually settled.
274	  - **Instance fields (S32).** `x.f` and `g[i].f` denote field `f` of an instance in `σ`. `g[i] is C` denotes `g[i].f is C` for the one field `f` of the machine whose type has the constructor `C`; with none or several such fields it is `PL1005`. Only configuration properties read instances' fields (PS1.6).
275	  - **`init(e)`** is the value of `e` in the configuration's initial state. Properties refer to initial quantities through `init`, never through constants explained in comments.
276	  - A **quiescent** global state has `μ` empty and no declared input accepted.
277	  - A **stuck** state is a quiescent state in which some non-service instance is not terminal. It is reported as `PL5402 STUCK`, the configuration's form of deadlock.
278	  - Liveness properties (`P leads to Q`) are checked under the delivery guarantee (PS14) and any stated fairness. In a configuration the fairness clause may be left out: delivery is fair by PS14.2, and an input is fair only if the clause names it (S56).
279	- **PS13.7** **Interpretations.** The three interpretations of PS4.1a apply to configurations unchanged:
280	  - **check** explores every input and every arrival order within the bounds;
281	  - **simulate** samples them (a Polytrion world, v2);
282	  - **run** is the deployed system.
283	
284	  The theorem of PS4.1b extends: every run of the deployed instances, whose inputs are in their domains and which stays within the bounds, is a path of the check interpretation, up to the choice of linearisation.
285	- **PS13.8** **The happens-before argument.** A deployed configuration does not execute a sequence of global steps. Instances step concurrently on different workers, and no one observes a global state. A run is a partial order of events under the causal relation `→`: a step precedes the next step of the same instance, and a send precedes the delivery of that message. The proof of PS13.7 is:
286	  1. **Commutation.** Every step touches one instance's state and adds messages to `μ`. So two steps of different instances that are unordered by `→` commute: applying them in either order gives the same global state.
287	  2. **Linear extensions.** Every linear extension of a run's partial order is therefore a sequence of global steps. It is a path of **check**, because **check** delivers any message in transit in any order (PS13.4).
288	  3. **Coverage.** A configuration invariant that holds on every path of **check** holds in every state of every linear extension, however the run is linearised. ∎
289	- **PS13.9** **Monitoring.** A configuration invariant is a statement about global states, which no participant observes. It constrains the system's behaviour, but no runtime monitor can check it directly. It is monitored either by taking a consistent snapshot of the instances (a cut closed under `→`) or offline, over the ledger, by replaying one linear extension of the recorded partial order.
290	
291	## PS14. Delivery
292	
293	- **PS14.1** **Every message sent is eventually received.** This is part of the meaning of `send`, not an assumption about a kernel. In a behaviour of a configuration, every message added to `μ` is eventually delivered. Every intent is eventually completed or refused. Every due timer eventually fires.
294	- **PS14.2** In the check interpretation, this is **weak fairness of each identified message's delivery**, realised in the explorer as weak fairness per value with oldest-copy delivery (PS13.2b). A message in transit stays deliverable until it is delivered, so weak fairness is enough. Liveness checks (PS6.4) include these fairness constraints automatically, so an author states only the fairness of the machines' own actions.
295	- **PS14.3** At runtime, delivery is obligation R1 (PS10). Delivery is at-least-once through the outbox, and the receiver deduplicates on the message's idempotency key (K4 with its lifetime). The claim that each message takes **exactly one step at its receiver** is a property of the delivery protocol. That protocol is modelled as the `Delivery` machine (PT9.8) and checked: at most one step per message always, at least one under fairness, and in-order delivery for the in-order worker. The runtime's conformance to that model is kernel assumption K8, checked by trace replay at M4.
296	
297	## Conclusion
298	
299	A poly program denotes a deterministic, labelled transition relation over a finite checked instance. Checking, simulation and running are three interpretations of one environment interface over that same relation, and the claim that the checked program is the running program is a theorem about two of them. States may be tagged unions, so invalid states are unrepresentable rather than merely unreachable. Policy logic has its own type. Machines talk to each other only by messages sent to addresses. A configuration of machines is checked with messages arriving in any order, within declared bounds. Delivery is part of what sending means, and the runtime is obliged to implement it. Attached children are co-located, and detached children are actors like any other. Obligations from all sources are checked together for a way to discharge each mandate; that check is a possibility property, named as such. Messages have identities, so fairness is per message, and the delivery protocol that makes a message take exactly one step is itself a checked machine. Rejections are labelled stuttering steps. Properties come in five kinds with distinct meanings. Liveness is stated only with its fairness assumptions. Policies have a total three-valued evaluation in which an unknown deny condition escalates. The lowering is correct when its transition relation equals this one, and every `poly check` verifies that for the program at hand. Every guarantee about a running program names the kernel assumptions it depends on.
300	// OutboxIntent in its v0.3 five-field form (03-technical-spec.md at commit 5160ba8).
301	// evidence/outbox_check.py v0.3: 33 states, 40 accepted steps, no deadlock.
302	module runtime
303	
304	enum IntentStatus { Pending, Proposed, Allowed, Running, Settled, Denied, Escalated, Dead, Done }
305	
306	machine OutboxIntent {
307	  state {
308	    status    : IntentStatus = Pending
309	    attempts  : 0..3         = 0
310	    decisions : 0..2         = 0     // gate decisions taken for this intent
311	    executed  : bool         = false // the handler may have run (at-least-once)
312	    approved  : bool         = false
313	  }
314	  terminal status in { Done, Denied, Dead }
315	
316	  action Propose()
317	  action GateAllow()
318	  action GateDeny()
319	  action GateEscalate()
320	  action Approve()
321	  action EscalationTimeout()
322	  action Start()
323	  action HandlerOk()
324	  action HandlerFailed()
325	  action SettleFailed()
326	  action SettleOk()
327	
328	  on Propose {
329	    require status in { Pending } || (status == Escalated && approved) else reject "not-proposable"
330	    status' = Proposed
331	    decisions' = decisions + 1
332	  }
333	  on GateAllow    { require status == Proposed else reject "no-proposal"   status' = Allowed }
334	  on GateDeny     { require status == Proposed else reject "no-proposal"
335	                    require !executed          else reject "deny-after-execution"
336	                    status' = Denied }
337	  on GateEscalate { require status == Proposed else reject "no-proposal"
338	                    require decisions == 1     else reject "escalate-once"
339	                    status' = Escalated }
340	  on Approve      { require status == Escalated else reject "not-escalated" approved' = true }
341	  on EscalationTimeout { require status == Escalated && !approved else reject "not-waiting"
342	                         status' = Denied }
343	  on Start        { require status == Allowed  else reject "not-allowed"
344	                    require attempts < 3       else reject "exhausted"
345	                    status' = Running
346	                    attempts' = attempts + 1
347	                    executed' = true }
348	  on HandlerOk    { require status == Running  else reject "not-running"   status' = Settled }
349	  on HandlerFailed { require status == Running else reject "not-running"
350	                     if attempts < 3 { status' = Allowed } else { status' = Dead } }
351	  on SettleFailed { require status == Settled  else reject "not-settled"
352	                    if attempts < 3 { status' = Allowed } else { status' = Dead } }
353	  on SettleOk     { require status == Settled  else reject "not-settled"   status' = Done }
354	
355	  invariant one-decision-per-execution: executed implies (decisions <= 1 || approved)
356	  step property no-reproposal-after-allow:
357	    pre.status in { Allowed, Running, Settled } implies post.status != Proposed
358	  step property no-deny-after-run: pre.executed implies post.status != Denied
359	  liveness settles: eventually status in { Done, Denied, Dead }
360	    under fair { Propose, GateAllow | GateDeny | GateEscalate, EscalationTimeout, Start,
361	                 HandlerOk | HandlerFailed, SettleOk | SettleFailed }
362	}
363	// PT9.8 as written: the in-order worker, and the dedupe table kept on archive (K4). delivery_check.py:
364	// 1,147 states, at-most-once and in-order hold; exactly-once is liveness, checked from M2.
365	module delivery
366	
367	type Msg = M1 | M2
368	type Status = Unsent | Pending | InFlight | Acked
369	
370	service machine Delivery {
371	  state {
372	    status   : map<Msg, Status> = { M1: Unsent, M2: Unsent }
373	    req      : map<Msg, 0..2>   = { M1: 0, M2: 0 }            // request copies in the network
374	    ack      : map<Msg, 0..2>   = { M1: 0, M2: 0 }            // acknowledgement copies in the network
375	    lost     : map<Msg, 0..1>   = { M1: 0, M2: 0 }            // the network loses at most one copy per message
376	    seen     : map<Msg, bool>   = { M1: false, M2: false }    // the receiver's dedupe table (K4)
377	    steps    : map<Msg, 0..2>   = { M1: 0, M2: 0 }            // steps taken at the receiver
378	    archived : bool = false
379	  }
380	  action Emit(m: Msg)     action Send(m: Msg)       action Resend(m: Msg)
381	  action LoseReq(m: Msg)  action DeliverReq(m: Msg) action LoseAck(m: Msg)
382	  action DeliverAck(m: Msg)  action Archive()
383	
384	  on Emit(m) {
385	    require status[m] == Unsent else reject "emitted"
386	    require m == M1 || status[M1] != Unsent else reject "emit-order"
387	    status' = status with [m] = Pending
388	  }
389	  on Send(m) {
390	    require status[m] == Pending && req[m] < 2 else reject "not-pending"
391	    require m == M1 || status[M1] == Acked else reject "in-order"      // the in-order worker
392	    status' = status with [m] = InFlight
393	    req' = req with [m] = req[m] + 1
394	  }
395	  on Resend(m) {
396	    require status[m] == InFlight && req[m] < 2 else reject "not-in-flight"
397	    req' = req with [m] = req[m] + 1
398	  }
399	  on LoseReq(m) {
400	    require req[m] > 0 && lost[m] < 1 else reject "no-loss"
401	    req' = req with [m] = req[m] - 1
402	    lost' = lost with [m] = 1
403	  }
404	  on DeliverReq(m) {
405	    require req[m] > 0 else reject "nothing-in-transit"
406	    req' = req with [m] = req[m] - 1
407	    if ack[m] < 2 { ack' = ack with [m] = ack[m] + 1 }
408	    if !seen[m] { seen' = seen with [m] = true
409	                  steps' = steps with [m] = steps[m] + 1 }
410	  }
411	  on LoseAck(m) {
412	    require ack[m] > 0 && lost[m] < 1 else reject "no-loss"
413	    ack' = ack with [m] = ack[m] - 1
414	    lost' = lost with [m] = 1
415	  }
416	  on DeliverAck(m) {
417	    require ack[m] > 0 else reject "no-ack"
418	    ack' = ack with [m] = ack[m] - 1
419	    if status[m] == InFlight { status' = status with [m] = Acked }
420	  }
421	  on Archive {
422	    require !archived && steps[M1] == 1 && steps[M2] == 1 else reject "not-done"
423	    archived' = true                                  // the dedupe table is kept (K4)
424	  }
425	
426	  invariant at-most-once: steps[M1] <= 1 && steps[M2] <= 1
427	  invariant in-order: steps[M2] >= 1 implies steps[M1] >= 1      // M2 never steps before M1 (S64)
428	  liveness exactly-once:
429	    eventually (status[M1] == Acked && status[M2] == Acked && steps[M1] == 1 && steps[M2] == 1)
430	    under fair { Emit(*), Send(*), Resend(*), DeliverReq(*), DeliverAck(*) }
431	}
